\Cref{thm:rootn} is our main result: the cross-fitted one-step is
$\sqrt n$-consistent and asymptotically normal with influence function
$J^{-1}\psi_\star$ and limiting variance $J^{-1}\Sigma J^{-1\prime}$, and the sample
sandwich $\hat V$ is consistent for it.

What carries the theorem is an *exact* decomposition rather than an expansion. The
bias decomposition of the supplement writes the conditional bias of the debiased
moment at the estimated nuisances as the balancing pairing
$-\langle\nu_{g_k}/\pi,h_k\rangle$ plus
exactly three remainders, one quadratic in the structural error and two products of
two estimation errors. There is no Taylor remainder in the weight or the propensity
directions, because the moment is bi-affine there. What makes each of the three
$o_P(n^{-1/2})$ is the frontier \eqref{eq:frontier}.

The empirical-process term costs nothing at scale $n^{-1/2}$, and that is a positioning
commitment rather than a technical convenience. Lemma L-8 of the supplement obtains
$\sqrt n\sum_{k=1}^{\mathsf F}\tfrac{n_k}{n}(\mathbb E_{n,k}-E)[\hat\psi^{(-k)}-\psi_\star]=o_P(1)$ from conditional
Chebyshev at a frozen nuisance, so the only input is $L^{2}(P)$-consistency of the
estimated moment: no entropy condition, no Donsker property, no stochastic
equicontinuity at the estimated point. We make that concession once, in the
$\varphi$-step, where we take a uniform law with a rate over a slowly growing
ball at scale $\hat\delta_n\gg n^{-1/2}$. A penalised
sieve minimum-distance treatment of $\theta$ would need the harder statement at the
harder scale.

The sandwich is simpler than its construction suggests. $J$ is defined as
the $\theta$-derivative of a two-summand moment, but under A1 the debiasing summand is the
zero matrix, so $J=E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']$ exactly and no rank condition beyond A1b(iv) is
needed anywhere (part (iv) of the moment-validity lemma of the supplement). As a
matter of fact the variance splits exactly, by the same tower step applied to the
cross term:
$\Sigma=E[\Delta Z\Delta Z'\Delta U^{2}]+E[L_\star\widetilde W\widetilde W'L_\star']$.
So the
sandwich is the variance the infeasible plug-in \eqref{eq:prelimtheta} would have at
a *known* $\vdagger$, plus a positive semidefinite term that does not vanish under
overlap.

That the second term does not vanish is reached differently at
$\mathsf L\ge3$, and the binary route is unavailable there rather than merely
weaker. At $\mathsf L=2$, $\widetilde W^{2}\ge\varepsilon_\varrho^{2}$ surely under
A4(i), which bounds the term below by $\varepsilon_\varrho^{2}E[L_\star L_\star']$.
At $\mathsf L\ge3$ that argument fails outright: $\widetilde W\widetilde W'$ has
rank one, so no sure inequality $\widetilde W\widetilde W'\succeq cI$ holds at any
$c>0$, and $L_\star\widetilde W\widetilde W'L_\star'$ is singular at every sample
point once $p>1$. The route that works at every $\mathsf L$ is the conditional
one, and it is what \eqref{eq:omegafloor} was written for: under A1,
$E[\widetilde W\widetilde W'\mid\Delta U,\Delta Z]=\Omega(\Delta Z)$, and A4(i)
gives $\Omega(\Delta Z)\succeq(\varepsilon_\varrho/\mathsf L)I$.

*What the debiasing weight buys is not variance but the removal of the first-order
bias* that the plug-in carries at exact order $\|h_k\|$. That is the standard
debiasing trade \citep[see][]{chernozhukov2022lr,ichimuranewey2022}, and it is not
a defect.

We do not compare the estimator to a semiparametric efficiency bound. The bound
\citet{poirier2017} computes under independence restrictions is for a model
without a structural inverse \citep[see also][]{aichen2012,bkrw1993}, and
computing one here, where the nuisance solves an ill-posed nonlinear operator
equation, is a step we leave to future research.

No correction for the estimation of $\varrho$ appears in the influence function, and its
absence is a consequence rather than an omission. By \cref{prp:orthog}(iii) the
$\varrho$-derivative of the moment vanishes exactly under N1, so there is nothing for a
correction to remove; Lemma L-11 of the supplement states this as a property of the
limit and not as an approximation to it.

The positivity the studentised statement needs is *implied by the theorem's hypotheses
rather than assumed*. Notice that its conclusion is quantified over every
$\vartheta$ with $\|\vartheta\|=1$, not over the directions on which the sandwich
happens to be positive. By part (v) of the moment-validity lemma of the supplement, $\Sigma\succ0$
follows from A1b(iv) and
C2$'$(i), both of which the theorem already carries, since
$E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']$ nonsingular gives $P(\vartheta'\Delta Z\ne0)>0$ and a
conditional density for $\Delta U$ gives $P(\Delta U=0)=0$.

A proviso that a theorem's hypotheses entail belongs in its conclusion and not on
the user's checklist.

The scope is mild ill-posedness, and severe ill-posedness is a place the theorem does not
reach rather than a gap in the proof. What \eqref{eq:frontier} requires is that $\delta_n$
be a *polynomial* rate faster than $n^{-1/4}$, which under H1's $\sigma_j\asymp j^{-a}$ is
what a source condition delivers. Under exponentially decaying singular values the
rate attainable from *any* source condition is logarithmic in $n$, so A5(ii) fails
at every $r$ and the theorem is unavailable.

H1's scale supplies a shorter reading of that scope, and it needs qualifying. The
reading pairs mild ill-posedness with $s>a+\tfrac12$, hence
$\mu>\tfrac12+1/(4a)$, and at $a\le\tfrac34$ that inequality is taken to deliver
the source-index restriction the theorem carries.

The inequalities in that reading are statements about $\mu_{\text{H1}}=s/(2a)$, the
index of A2 at the *population* operator on all of $\mathcal V$ at $\theta_\dagger$, whereas
\eqref{eq:muhalf} and \eqref{eq:frontier} carry (P-a.3)'s primitive $\mu$ at the
finite-rank compression of the realised operator at $\theta_\circ$. The bridge
between them is the operator interpolation that the supplement's remark on (P-a.3)
shows unavailable at every $2\mu>1$, and the commutativity proviso that would
restore it is stated and declined.

Read as an interpretation it is right; read as a scope statement it both excludes
designs the theorem covers and claims designs it does not.

The rate condition cannot be relaxed by bounding the remainder more carefully, *and that
is a weaker claim than necessity*. By \cref{prp:sharpquad} the supremum of the second-order
remainder over an $L^{2}(\pi)$-ball of radius $\delta$ in $\mathcal V$ is exactly
$\tfrac12\delta^{2}$ times the norm of the compressed symmetrised form, which is strictly
positive under O-16(a). So the direct bound is order-sharp, and no argument that
merely improves it will weaken \eqref{eq:frontier}.

The sharpness statement invites readings that the supplement's scope remark blocks.
It does not
say that the realised remainder at $h_k=\hat\varphi^{(-k)}-\vdagger$ fails to be
$o_P(\|h_k\|^{2})$: a regularisation path confined to directions on which the form
is small could do better, and nothing here excludes that. It does not say that
$\delta_n=o(n^{-1/4})$ is *necessary* for $\sqrt n$-estimability of $\theta_\dagger$
by some estimator. And it does not say the moment class is exhausted.

What relaxing the frontier would require is a different selection, one with a
smaller $\sigma_q$ and compact part, which is open. The alternative is a restriction
on the *direction* of the first-stage error, which is an extra hypothesis and not a
sharper argument. The sharpness statement carries a hypothesis of its own, O-16, which asserts that
the form does not degenerate and which does not follow from \cref{cor:udep}. Here
$q$ can vanish by cancellation inside the conditional expectation, and
$q\not\equiv0$ alone is not enough either, an antisymmetric $q\,f_{X_1,X_2}$ making
the form vanish against the symmetric $(\Delta h)^{2}$.

*We acknowledge that near the frontier the theorem's asymptotics do not bind at any
sample size anyone will run, and we would rather say so than let a referee find it.*

Write $\hat\delta_n=n^{-\alpha}$ and $\kappa=2\mu/(2\mu+1)$. The $\theta$-remainder is
$O_P(n^{-1/2}+\sqrt n\,\delta_n^{2})$ and its second term is
$\sqrt n\,\delta_n^{2}=n^{-\beta}(\ln n)^{2\kappa}$ with $\beta=2\kappa\alpha-\tfrac12$,
which is strictly positive by \eqref{eq:frontier}. In $t=\ln n$ that is
$e^{-\beta t}t^{2\kappa}$, which is *increasing* for $t<2\kappa/\beta$, so the remainder
*rises* in $n$ up to $n^{\ast}=\exp\{2\kappa/\beta\}$ and only then falls. The
Monte Carlo experiment at the configuration this theory names, which the
supplement carries, runs at $\mu=2$, hence $\kappa=\tfrac45$, and at
$\alpha=0.32$, so that $\kappa\alpha=0.256>\tfrac14$ and the design sits *inside* the
frontier. There one gets $\beta=0.012$ and $n^{\ast}=e^{400/3}\approx10^{58}$.

That threshold is a fact about where the design sits and not about the theorem, and the
same formula prices designs that sit elsewhere. It is not an artefact of a badly chosen
parameterisation: $\beta\downarrow0$ as $\kappa\alpha\downarrow\tfrac14$, so
$n^{\ast}\uparrow\infty$ at the frontier and the $10^{58}$ is a property of
\eqref{eq:frontier} itself. But $n^{\ast}$ falls away from the frontier as steeply as it
climbs towards it, and it does so well inside the admissible range rather than at its edge.

Take $d_Z=1$. A first stage with $r=5$ derivatives gives $\alpha=\tfrac5{11}$, hence
$\beta=\tfrac5{22}$ and $n^{\ast}=e^{176/25}\approx1{,}140$ at $\mu=2$, and
$n^{\ast}=e^{352/61}\approx320$ at $\mu=4$; at $r=12$ and $\mu=10$,
$n^{\ast}=e^{400/87}\approx99$. These are ordinary smooth designs with a scalar
conditioning variable, satisfying every hypothesis the theorem carries, and at them the turn
happens at sample sizes anyone will run.
*So the concession is that the asymptotics do not bind near the frontier, and that
the configuration that experiment runs is near it.* It is not that they bind nowhere.

Nothing in this weakens \eqref{eq:rootn}. The $o_P(1)$ there is a statement
about the limit and it is proved. What changes is how finite-sample evidence should be
read. Below $n^{\ast}$ the object that describes the estimator is
\cref{cor:ratefloor}, in which $\delta_n^{2}$, $\delta_n\epsilon_n$, $r_n\delta_n$ and
$r_n\epsilon^{L}_n$ appear as *terms* of the rate and not as remainders sent to zero, and
\eqref{eq:rootn} is the special case in which every term after $n^{-1/2}$ is
$o(n^{-1/2})$.

That corollary is honest about its own exponents in the same way. On the branch that
prices $\hat\ell$ directly, two of them, $\epsilon_n$ and $\epsilon^{L}_n$, are
assumed and not derived, because neither has a supplier in the maintained block.
Only on the sieve branch for the first-order bias, together with N1$'$ at each
estimated direction, do both unsupplied symbols disappear. What is in primitives is
then not \eqref{eq:ratefloor} but the display that replaces it,
$\delta_n\epsilon_n$ giving way to
$O_P(n^{-1/2}\delta_n)+O_P(\mathsf R\,L_x^{-s})$ and $r_n\epsilon^{L}_n$ dropping
out, every exponent of which is a function of $(\mu,r,d_Z,s)$.

So the correct reading of \eqref{eq:frontier} is that it is a *qualitative*
frontier: crossing it makes the remainder vanish eventually and says nothing about
where.

Finally, the theorem is *pointwise in $P$*, and this is the quantifier the finite-sample
caveats all sit inside. Every hypothesis is imposed at a single data-generating law, and
$\mu$, $\mathsf R_\ast$, $a$, $s$, $\varepsilon_\varrho$, $r$, $\bar c_\pi$, the
representer's budgets and the singular system of $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ are all
$P$-specific constants.

The consequences are real limitations rather than formalities. The $o_P(1)$ in
\eqref{eq:rootn} is not uniform over any neighbourhood of $P$, so the theorem does not
deliver confidence sets whose coverage is honest over a class, and no such class is
defined here. The $10^{58}$ of the previous paragraph is that gap displayed numerically:
within any class containing laws arbitrarily close to the frontier the convergence cannot
be uniform. And $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)>0$ holds at each $P$ and may be arbitrarily
small along a sequence of laws, so the positivity established above is pointwise too.

A uniform statement would need a class on which those constants are bounded, a
uniform version of \eqref{eq:phirate} at a random compressed operator, and a
Lindeberg condition uniform in $P$. We attempt none of the three.
